idiom_name: predicate '?' / dangerous '!' method-name suffixes and attr_reader query macros
implementation_notes: Ruby carries intent inside the method name itself: a name may end in `?` (predicate - ruby-doc.org documents that such methods return a boolean-like value, and the core library guarantees it for `Array#empty?`, `Object#nil?`) or in `!` (dangerous: `Hash#merge!` mutates the receiver while `merge` returns a new hash), and `attr_reader`/`attr_accessor` turn instance variables into named queries instead of hand-written `get_x` methods. Those suffixes are syntax and the semantics are convention - the parser accepts `?` on any method and nothing forces a predicate to return a boolean - so the signifier is only as honest as the author. Keep the hand-written reader (`def total_in_minor_units`) when the accessor computes, validates or memoises, and reserve `!` for a method that genuinely has a non-bang counterpart.
code_sketch:
class Order
  attr_reader :lines                    # named query, no get_/set_ pair

  def cancellable? = status == :draft              # predicate: boolean-like, no side effects
  def total_in_minor_units = lines.sum(&:amount)   # query: no side effects

  def add_line(sku:, quantity:)                    # command: verb, mutates receiver
    raise OrderClosed if submitted?
    lines << OrderLine.new(sku: sku, quantity: quantity)
  end
end
pitfalls: A predicate that lazily loads, memoises or mutates breaks callers that use it in `if` conditions and test assertions; `?` promises a cheap boolean-like answer, so keep side effects out.
Bang methods without a non-bang counterpart (or the reverse) are the standard Ruby naming failure: `Array#flatten!` returns `nil` when nothing changed, so `x = arr.flatten!` silently loses the value.

`method_missing`/`define_method`-generated methods hide the surface from `respond_to?` and from documentation; implement `respond_to_missing?` and document the generated names so the interface stays inspectable.
